messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Linh

Linh was thirty-one when her mother died. It happened on a Tuesday morning in March, without warning—a sudden cardiac arrhythmia while her mother was at work, alone in her office. Linh learned about it from a hospital administrator's phone call, delivered while she sat in the newsroom of the Seattle Tribune, mid-sentence in an email to her editor. One moment she was a journalist with a byline and a divorce that was almost final; the next moment she was someone whose mother had stopped breathing and there was nothing—no sign, no illness, no time to say anything at all.

The funeral was held in Portland, where her mother had lived since remarrying five years earlier. Linh delivered a eulogy that felt like reading someone else's words. She returned to Seattle three days later and went back to work because she did not know what else to do. Her editor gave her two weeks off. She took four days.

Within weeks, Linh noticed that her body had become a stranger to her. She could not sit through a full news meeting without her heart rate spiking, without the sensation of being perched on the edge of a chair even when she was sitting squarely in it. Her colleagues would chat about weekend plans, and she would feel the muscles across her shoulders and neck tighten as though bracing for impact. At home, in the evenings, she found herself unable to settle into the couch with a book or a show. She would start to relax—her breathing would deepen, her shoulders would drop—and then something would shift. A car door would slam outside. A notification would buzz on her phone. Her mind would leap to catastrophe. *Something is wrong. Someone else is dying. You should be ready.* She would stand up, pace, check her phone, refresh her news feeds, as though vigilance itself might prevent the next unbearable loss.

What frightened her most was the randomness of it all. Her mother had been healthy. Fifty-eight years old, active, no family history of cardiac disease. She had gone to work that morning and never come home. This fact—that death could arrive without announcement, without mercy, without any warning at all—had reorganized Linh's entire nervous system. She had come to believe that the only way to survive was to remain alert, to monitor the environment constantly for signs of danger, to never allow herself the vulnerability of genuine rest. To relax was to lower her guard, and to lower her guard was to invite another catastrophe she would be powerless to stop.

The hypervigilance had become exhausting. At the Tribune, Linh found herself scanning colleagues' faces during meetings, alert to any sign of distress or illness. She would notice if someone seemed quieter than usual and immediately assume the worst. She began researching rare cardiac conditions on her laptop between assignments, reading case studies of sudden deaths in young, seemingly healthy people. She attended her mother's cardiologist's memorial service—a gesture that confused her colleagues—and asked the physician detailed questions about screening protocols, as though understanding the mechanisms of sudden death might somehow grant her control over it.

Her ex-husband had called in early May, checking in. She could hear the discomfort in his voice, the careful distance he maintained even in his concern. They had divorced two years earlier, and the separation had been amicable but thorough. Now, when he asked how she was managing, Linh heard herself giving short answers. She did not tell him that she was sleeping only in fragments, that she would wake at 3 a.m. with her heart racing, convinced something had happened to her father or her younger brother. She did not tell him that she had started calling her brother every morning, ostensibly to chat, but really to confirm he was still alive. She did not tell him that the thought of being alone—truly alone, with no one to monitor, no one to check on—filled her with a dread so acute it made her hands shake.

It was her editor who finally insisted. Linh had missed a deadline in July, something she had never done in eight years at the paper. She had been in the middle of a feature when a colleague mentioned his father's upcoming bypass surgery, and Linh had frozen at her desk, unable to type, unable to think of anything but the fragility of the human heart. Her editor pulled her into his office and said, quietly, that she needed to talk to someone. He gave her the name of a therapist who specialized in grief and trauma. Linh made the appointment because she was afraid of losing her job, but also because she was afraid of what her body might do next if she did not find a way to make it stop—this constant, exhausting vigilance, this inability to trust that she was safe even in the safest moments of her life.
